scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Modern line dance emerged in the 20th century, with roots in European folk dances brought to North America in the 1800s.
The 1957 'Madison' is considered one of the first true line dances.

The 1970s disco era introduced dances like the 'L.A. Hustle' and 'Electric Slide', while the 1980s and 90s saw a surge in country-western line dancing, popularized by films like 'Urban Cowboy' and songs like 'Achy Breaky Heart'.
on_screen: Map: United States · Global

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Line dance serves as a social activity and a form of recreational exercise.
It is used in dance programs alongside other styles and is recognized as a competitive discipline in some regions.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Line-Dance Videos (https://archive.org/details/Line-danceVideos)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers stand in rows, repeating a set sequence of steps.
Movements are performed independently without physical contact.
Choreographies are often based on counts of 32, 48, or 64, with syncopated steps like shuffles or chassés.
Watch for Shuffle, Turn.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Originally tied to country-western music, line dance now incorporates pop, disco, Latin, rock, and techno.
Instruments vary by genre, but the music must be suitable for a repeating, rhythmic step sequence.
Music is chosen for its suitability to a repeating, rhythmic step sequence, spanning genres from country to pop and disco.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Ric L. Silver (choreographer of the Electric Slide), Max Perry, Jo Thompson Szymanski, Scott Blevins, and Bill Bader.
Variations include contra-dance (lines facing each other), and regional styles influenced by local music scenes in the US, Europe, and Quebec.
Evolved from 19th-century European folk dances and 20th-century show dance.
